figures.title: What the decoder actually receives
figures.caption: Hidden width 256. Five source tokens carry 1,280 floats of embeddings, fifty carry 12,800, and the summary has 256 slots for either. The strips are drawn to one scale, so the solid head is the same size in both plain-seq2seq rows and the dashed remainder is what the decoder never sees. Bahdanau keeps every annotation instead, so its strip is solid end to end.
figures.alt: Three to-scale strips sharing one horizontal scale. Plain seq2seq with five source tokens: a 1,280-float strip whose solid 256-float head is labelled 256 floats survive and whose dashed remainder is labelled 1,280 discarded. Plain seq2seq with fifty source tokens: a strip ten times longer, the same 256-float head, 12,800 discarded. Bahdanau attention with fifty tokens: the whole 12,800 floats kept and read at every decoder step.

data.note: The gradient is the other half of the bottleneck. Back through T recurrent steps the derivative is a product of T−1 Jacobians; with each factor 0.4, twenty steps give 0.4^19 ≈ 2.7 × 10^-8.

figures.title: Additive scoring versus one dot-product matrix
figures.caption: At n = 20 decoder steps, m = 50 source positions, k = 128 and d = 512, additive scoring costs about 7.86M multiply-adds for the projections plus 128,000 for the per-pair dot, roughly 8M. Dot-product scoring costs 20 × 50 × 1024 = 1,024,000, about 16 times less. The penalty is the shape of the work: additive evaluates a tanh per pair over a k × n × m intermediate, dot-product is one GEMM producing one n × m sheet.
figures.alt: Two panels sharing one scale. Additive attention draws a stack of 128 sheets, one per k, each an n by m sheet of per-pair tanh evaluations, with a depth bracket labelled k = 128 sheets; the front sheet carries e = vᵀ tanh(W₁h_j + W₂s_i), and beneath it the cost ≈ 7.86M + 0.128M ≈ 8M multiply-adds. Dot product draws a single n by m sheet labelled S Hᵀ, with 20 × 50 × 1024 = 1,024,000 multiply-adds and the note that it is about 16 times less arithmetic.

data.note: Both sides are matrix multiplies. The difference is that additive materialises a k × n × m intermediate and then reduces it, while dot product produces its result in one GEMM.

panels.title: additive (Bahdanau 2014)
panels.note: A tanh per pair, elementwise and memory-bound. A fused implementation can avoid materialising the full tensor, but then it cannot batch into one large multiply.

panels.title: dot product (Luong 2015; Vaswani 2017)
panels.note: One GEMM, one sheet, ≈ 16× less arithmetic at these lengths. The ratio shifts with n and m because the projection cost amortizes.

anim.intro: Press Play or Next to compare the two shapes of work.

steps.label: Additive precomputes two projections, then evaluates a tanh over every pair.
That is a k-deep stack, 128 sheets of n × m, materialised and then reduced.
Dot product folds both sides into one GEMM: S Hᵀ is a single n × m sheet.
≈ 8M against 1,024,000. About 16 times less arithmetic, and one operation instead of a stack.

figures.title: Softmax sharpens the weights; the alignment story is ours
figures.caption: Three annotations scored 2.0, 1.0 and 0.0 get softmax shares 0.665, 0.245 and 0.090. Raising the first score to 4.0 gives 0.936, 0.047 and 0.017: the distribution sharpens toward a hard choice without becoming one. The weights are real numbers the model computed; reading them as word alignments is an interpretation, and Koehn and Knowles show it does not reliably hold.
figures.alt: Six horizontal bars in two labelled groups on one scale. Before: h₁ scored 2.0 has weight 0.665, h₂ scored 1.0 has 0.245, h₃ scored 0.0 has 0.090. After raising h₁ to 4.0: h₁ has 0.936, h₂ has 0.047, h₃ has 0.017. The second group is sharper but still spread over all three.

data.note: e^2, e^1, e^0 = 7.389, 2.718, 1.000, sum 11.107. Raise h₁ to 4.0: 54.598, 2.718, 1.000, sum 58.316. The softmax gradient keeps a baseline, so the weights' score gradient sums to zero across source positions.

The weights become 0.936, 0.047, 0.017. Sharper, still not a hard choice.
